title: How do the primes of two numbers build their lowest common multiple?
description: The numbers fourteen and thirty five are written as products of primes, and a common multiple is built that holds both products as subparts, sharing the seven. Removing any prime breaks one of the numbers. Keeko doubts this and wants to multiply fourteen and thirty five, which uses the seven twice.
teaching_notes: One idea: a common multiple must hold the prime product of each number as a subpart, and a shared prime can serve both numbers. Watch for students who multiply the two numbers and use a shared prime twice.

source: Find the LCM of 14 and 35 from their prime factorisations.
video_script.why: The child can find a lowest common multiple by listing multiples and needs a quicker way from the prime products when the lists get long.
video_script.substitution: Build the smallest product of primes that holds each number's primes as a subpart, sharing the primes the numbers have in common.
video_script.anchor: The prime products 14 = 2 × 7 and 35 = 5 × 7 written one under the other with the shared 7 lined up, as in the book's example.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko multiplies fourteen and thirty five to get four hundred ninety, which uses the seven twice, though one seven can serve both numbers.
video_script.payoff_line: The lowest common multiple is seventy
never_show: 490 as the lowest common multiple, marked right
maths_rules: a common multiple must contain 2 × 7 as a subpart and 5 × 7 as a subpart
removing any prime from 2 × 5 × 7 breaks one of them, so it is the lowest
slip: 14 × 35 = 490 = 7 × 70, a common multiple but not the lowest; it uses 7 twice
video_script.design: One idea: a common multiple must hold each number's primes as a subpart, and a shared prime is used once. The two prime products stay on the board from step one to the answer.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We must find a number that both fourteen and thirty five divide.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The lowest such number is called the lowest common multiple.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Each number is a product of primes. How can those primes build the lowest common multiple?

beats.on_screen: the two numbers stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 and its multiple 648 = (2 × 2 × 3 × 3) × (2 × 3 × 3), the first product boxed inside the second and labelled subpart

marks.m2: the product for 648 appears with the product for 36 boxed inside it
marks.m4: the extra primes outside the box are lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Compare thirty six with one of its multiples, six hundred forty eight.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The primes of thirty six sit inside the primes of the multiple.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A piece taken from a product of primes is called a subpart.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Every multiple holds the primes of the number as a subpart, along with some more primes.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the two numbers fourteen and thirty five.

beats.on_screen: To find: the LCM of 14 and 35

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find their lowest common multiple.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: write each number as a product of primes: 14 = 2 × 7; 35 = 5 × 7

marks.m1: the words product of primes are written
marks.m3: 35 = 5 × 7 is written under it with the sevens lined up

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, write each number as a product of primes.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Fourteen is two times seven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Thirty five is five times seven.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: a common multiple must hold 2 × 7 as a subpart and 5 × 7 as a subpart

marks.m1: 2 × 7 is boxed as the first subpart
marks.m2: 5 × 7 is boxed as the second subpart

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, a common multiple must hold two times seven as a subpart.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It must also hold five times seven as a subpart.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: share the 7: 2 × 5 × 7 holds both 2 × 7 and 5 × 7; removing any prime breaks one of them

marks.m1: the two sevens slide together into one 7
marks.m2: 2 × 5 × 7 is written with both subparts boxed inside it
marks.m3: each prime is crossed out in turn and one box breaks

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, one seven can serve both subparts, so share it.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two times five times seven holds both subparts.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Take away any prime, and one of the numbers no longer fits. This is the lowest one.

marks.m1: the primes slide together and LCM = 2 × 5 × 7 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, multiply the primes, two, five and seven.

marks.m1: the answer is written and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The lowest common multiple is seventy.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Seventy is five fourteens, and also two thirty fives.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the two prime products
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 14 × 35 = 490 with two 7s; 490 = 7 × 70; the bubble is struck out and 70 returns

marks.m3: 490 = 7 × 70 is written and the bubble is struck out

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks we get it by multiplying fourteen and thirty five, which gives four hundred ninety.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That uses the seven twice, but only one seven is needed.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Four hundred ninety is a common multiple, but it is seven times seventy.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>One seven can serve both numbers, so a smaller number works. The answer stays seventy.
